newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: St. Helena bids for piece of tourism pie.
newsitem.headline: St. Helena bids for piece of tourism pie.

text.p: The tiny Atlantic Ocean island of St. Helena on Sunday launched a yacht race they hope will win it a slice of the world's burgeoning exotic tourism market.

Island governor David Smallman signalled the start in Cape Town's Table Bay of the first Governor's Cup, sending 12 South African yachts on the downwind chase likely to take the fastest boats about 10 days.
The fleet was sent off by the German Navy's stately square-rigged sailing ship Gorch Fock, which is on a round-the-world training mission for 115 cadets.
Cadets swarmed through the rigging to unfurl 15 sails as the ship followed the racers for a short distance, before returning to anchor as the yachts disappeared over the horizon in a near gale.
"St. Helena is on neither the world yachting charts nor the international tourist maps," Smallman said aboard the island's small passenger liner, St. Helena.
"We very much hope that this inaugural Cape Town to St. Helena yacht race will once more put St. Helena indelibly into the minds of travellers," he said.
St. Helena, best known as the place where Napoleon was exiled after his defeat in the battle of Waterloo, is a volcanic island almost halfway between Angola and Brazil. It is administered by Britain.

The race was conceived by Captain David Roberts, master of the 105-metre (344 ft) Royal Mail Ship St. Helena, as a way to drum up business for his vessel, which is the island's main cargo lifeline and also carries up to 128 passengers.
Roberts will bring six of the yachts back to Cape Town after the race, leaving the others to continue on longer voyages or to sail back.
